en: The Mahāyāna Śālistamba Sūtra,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Dharma Master Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Furthermore, there was an assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with the Bodhisattva Maitreya as their leader.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having observed Śāriputra, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If there is a bhikṣu who can clearly perceive and understand dependent origination through its twelve links, this is called 'seeing the Dharma'."
"Having seen this Dharma, one is said to have seen the Buddha.
After the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, Śāriputra immediately thought to himself:
"Now that our World-Honored One has preached such a Dharma,
what is its meaning?
How should it be understood?"

He immediately went to where the Bodhisattva Maitreya was; having arrived and met him, they exchanged polite greetings with gentle words and sat together beneath a large rock with the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
Then Śāriputra addressed Maitreya, saying:
"The World-Honored One has now taught the *Śālistambasūtra* to the bhikṣus, stating:
'Bhikṣus, if one is able to see dependent origination in its twelve links, this is called seeing the Dharma;'"
"Having seen these dharmas, one is said to have seen the Buddha. O Bodhisattva!
I do not now understand this meaning.
What is called the twelvefold dependent origination?
What is called the Dharma?
And what is called the Buddha?
"I only pray that the Bodhisattva will briefly explain this for us!
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, possesses all-encompassing wisdom; what he has spoken according to the needs of beings is profoundly deep and subtle."
You have now questioned me, and I shall now explain it briefly. Śāriputra!
As the Blessed One has said:
"If there is a bhikṣu who is able to clearly perceive dependent origination in its twelve links, this is called seeing the Dharma;
if one sees this Dharma, it is called seeing the Buddha."

"Śāriputra! As for dependent origination in twelve links: namely, ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
Thus, with this arising, there arises this entire great mass of suffering."

Śāriputra! With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. Through such cessation, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
"Śāriputra! Thus has the Blessed One spoken regarding dependent origination. Śāriputra said:
"What is called the Dharma?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"The Noble Eightfold Path is called the Dharma; namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
“Śāriputra! This Nirvāṇa is the fruit and retribution of the Eightfold Noble Path; therefore, the World-Honored One briefly designates it as ‘Dharma. Śāriputra said:
"What is meant by 'Buddha'?
The Bodhisattva replied,
"One who knows all phenomena is called a Buddha."
Thus, having attained the noble eye of wisdom and seeing the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), one realizes the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, how does one see the twelve links of dependent origination?
As the Buddha has said:

"If a person constantly perceives these twelve links of dependent origination as being without arising, without cessation, unconditioned, uncreated, without grasping, without attachment, real, non-perverted, quiescent, fearless, supreme, inexhaustible, cessation, and entirely devoid of intrinsic nature—if one sees them thus, that person sees the Dharma.

If one can thus constantly perceive them as without arising, without cessation, unconditioned, uncreated, without grasping, without attachment, real, non-perverted, quiescent, fearless, supreme, inexhaustible, cessation, and see the Dharma as devoid of intrinsic nature, that person sees the unsurpassed Dharmakāya."
“The Buddha is one who has attained the True Dharma, Right Wisdom, and the Samādhi of Cessation.
Furthermore, Śāriputra said:
“For what reason is it called ‘the twelve links of dependent origination’?”
The Bodhisattva said:
"Because there are causes and because there are conditions, it is called 'twelvefold dependent origination. Śāriputra!"
This Dharma is neither cause nor condition, yet it is also not without cause or condition; furthermore, it arises from conditions.
I shall now briefly explain its characteristics.

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, this law of causes and conditions remains eternally abiding, equal, as-it-is, and non-illusory; it is the true Dharma because it is free from inversion.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
This dependent origination is divided into two meanings. What are these two?
The first is arising from causes, and the second is arising from conditions.
These two meanings are divided into internal and external.

Regarding external conditions arising from causes: this refers to the production of a sprout from a seed, a stalk from a sprout, a stem from a stalk, branches and leaves from a stem, and flowers and fruit from branches and leaves.
If there is no seed, then the sprout will not arise, and even the flower and fruit will not exist.
If there is a seed, then the sprout and stem will arise, and even the flower and fruit will all be present.
Śāriputra! That seed does not form the thought:
"I am able to produce the sprout."
The sprout also does not form the thought:
"I am able to produce the stalk.
In this manner, it continues until even the flower does not form the thought: [“I am able to produce the fruit”].
"The flower thinks, 'I can produce the fruit,' yet the fruit also does not form the thought,
'I can be produced from the flower.'"
"In this way, external dependent origination as phenomena arising from causes can be seen.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
that which is external dependent origination arising from conditions refers to the convergence of the six elements."
What are the six elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the time element.

Among these, the earth element provides stability, the water element provides moisture, the fire element provides warmth, the wind element provides motion, the space element provides non-obstruction, and the time element brings about accomplishment.
In this way, when these six elements each meet with their respective conditions, the seed is able to produce sprouts, stalks, flowers, and fruit, all without deficiency.
If even one of these six elements does not come together, the seed will not grow, and even the flowers and fruit cannot be obtained.
However, among those six elements, each is devoid of a self; that earth element does not say,
"I am able to establish [the body]," nor does the water element say:
"I can moisten," says the water; nor does fire say, "I can warm."
The wind also does not say,
"I am able to move and shake.
Space also does not say:
"I am unimpeded," he does not say at that time; nor does he say,
"I can achieve [it]."
Yet that seed does not say,
"I am able to produce the sprout," nor does the sprout say:
"I arise from various conditions.

Thus, that which is produced, such as a sprout, is not self-made, not made by another, nor produced by a combination of self and other; it is not emanated by Īśvara, nor produced by time, nor born of conditions alone, nor produced by a single cause, nor is it produced without a cause.

However, that [result] arises from earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, as well as seeds, flowers, and fruits; it is neither identical to nor separate from them, and because it is subject to neither exhaustion nor extinction.
"Furthermore, dependent origination has five further meanings.
What are these five? They are:
it is neither eternal nor annihilated; although it ceases, it is not exhausted; a small cause produces a great fruit; and factors serve as mutual objects of perception."
Why is it not eternal?
Because the seed and the sprout have different names.
Why is it not discontinuous?
This means that from the seed there is the sprout, and from the sprout grow the branches and leaves.
How is it that although they perish, they are not exhausted?
"Although they perish" means that when the seed decays, it appears to have perished.
That which is not exhausted refers to the transmission of the seed that produces the sprout.
How is it that there is a small cause and a great fruit?
It means that with a single seed as the cause, the resulting fruit is manifold and doubled.
How do they serve as mutual objects of cognition?
It means that because of the seed there is the sprout, and so on up to the flower and fruit; these similar links in succession further become seeds themselves.
Furthermore, what are the twelve internal dependent originations?
These twelve links of dependent origination further possess two meanings.
What are these two? They are:
first, arising from causes; second, arising from conditions.
What is meant by "conditioned by causes"?
It is that conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise; and so on, up to birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
If there were no ignorance, volitional formations would not arise; likewise, up to aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair would not exist.
Yet that ignorance does not form the thought:
"I am able to produce volitional formations."
Furthermore, formative action does not give rise to the thought:
"I am born from ignorance," and so on, up to:
birth does not give rise to the thought: [“I am born from becoming”].
"I am able to produce birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
Nor do old age, death, and the rest form the thought:
"I arise from birth."
This is called the characteristic of that which arises from causes.
What is it that arises from conditions?
It refers to the attainment of the harmony of the six elements through conditions.
What are these six?
They are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
When these six elements combine, this is called "arising from conditions."
What is called the earth element?
It refers to the solidity of the body; this is called the earth element.
If the body is moist, this is called the water element.
If there is warmth in the body, this is called the fire element;
if there is inhalation and exhalation, this is called the wind element;
if there is non-obstruction within the body, this is called the space element.
From eye-consciousness up to the eighth consciousness, these are called the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*).
Through the conjunction of conditions among these six elements, the body is produced.
Yet, the earth element does not form the thought:
"I am able to provide solidity," nor does the water element form the thought,
"I am able to provide moisture."
The fire element also does not form the thought:
"I am able to provide warmth.
The wind element also does not form the thought:
The space element also does not form the thought:
"I am able to provide no obstruction."
Consciousness, too, does not form the thought:
"I am able to accomplish this.
The body, too, does not form the thought:
"I am born from a multitude of conditions.
Yet, apart from these conditions, the body does not exist.
Furthermore, that earth element is without self, without person, without sentient being, without life-span; it is neither male nor female, and it is neither self nor other.

Even down to the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness, there is no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-span; it is neither male nor female, and there is neither self nor other.

Furthermore, if one forms conceptions regarding these six elements—such as the conception of unity, the conception of an ordinary person, the conception of permanence, the conception of reality, the conception of duration, the conception of pleasure, the conception of a self, the conception of a person, the conception of a sentient being, the conception of a life-span, or the conception of a moving creature—and because of a lack of wisdom forms such various conceptions, this is therefore called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Due to ignorance (*avidyā*), greed and hatred arise. Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);
these formations likewise cling to provisional designations, and the arising of various conceptualizations is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
From the arising of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arises.
From name-and-form arise the six sense bases;
from the six sense bases arises contact;
because of contact, sensation arises.
From sensation arises craving;
from craving arises grasping;
from grasping arises becoming.
Because they exist, the subsequent aggregates are able to arise; this arising is called "birth.
Once arisen, their decay and transformation is "aging.
The disintegration of the aggregates is "death."
Due to delusion, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction arise.
Furthermore, because various sufferings gather and press upon the body and mind, dwelling in great darkness is called ignorance (*avidyā*);
the act of conditioning is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Discrimination is consciousness;
the establishment of characteristics is name-and-form;
the six sense-faculties as gateways are the six sense bases.
Contact with objects is called "contact" (sparśa);
the experience of pleasure and pain is called "feeling" (vedanā);
hunger and thirst are called "craving" (tṛṣṇā).
The pursuit of name-and-form is *upādāna*;
the subsequent arising of karma is *bhava*;
and the subsequent arising of the aggregates is *jāti*.
The maturation of the aggregates is aging;
their disintegration is death;
and the anxiety of reflection is sorrow.
Piteous distress is sorrow;
the multitude of sufferings is suffering;
and weariness and agitation are affliction.
Furthermore, to invert reality and regard it as false, and to take wrong views for right views—because this constitutes a lack of wisdom, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
There are three kinds of formations (*saṃskāra*): namely, meritorious formations, non-meritorious formations, and formations of the signless (*animitta*).

One gains knowledge of meritorious formations through performing meritorious formations; one gains knowledge of non-meritorious formations through performing non-meritorious formations; and one gains knowledge of signless formations through performing signless formations.
This continues in the same manner up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

Each of these twelve links of dependent origination has its own cause and its own fruit; they are neither eternal nor annihilated, neither conditioned nor separate from the conditioned, neither mental phenomena nor subject to exhaustion, nor subject to cessation; they are inherently self-existent, and that which is produced therein is uninterrupted.
"It is like a great river, flowing on without interruption.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Those twelve links of dependent origination are further increased by four conditions, namely: ignorance, craving, karma, and consciousness."
That seed of consciousness has its own nature as its cause, karma as its soil, and is covered by ignorance, craving, and afflictions; thus the seed of consciousness arises.
That karma serves as the ground for consciousness, craving provides moisture for consciousness, and with ignorance as a covering, consciousness achieves its formation.
That karma does not form the thought:
"I am able to serve as the ground for the seed of consciousness."
Craving also does not think:
"I am able to provide moisture for the seed of consciousness.
Ignorance also does not think:
"I am able to act as a covering for the seed of consciousness.
For this reason, the seed of consciousness is brought to fulfillment.
Furthermore, consciousness does not form the thought:
"I am born from a multitude of conditions.

Furthermore, with karma as the soil for consciousness, craving as the moisture, and ignorance as the covering, the seed is produced; within the mother's womb, it becomes the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

That sprout of name-and-form is not produced by itself, nor produced by another, nor produced by both self and other together; it is not produced by the Lord (Īśvara), nor produced by the transformation of time, nor born from a primal source, nor produced without causes and conditions.
This phenomenon truly arises from the union of parents and various conditions.
Yet that sprout of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) originally has no master, nor is there any grasping or rejecting; its self-nature and causal conditions are like space or a magical illusion.
"Furthermore, there are five causes and conditions for the arising of visual consciousness.
What are these five? They are:
the eye, visible forms, illumination, space, and mental attention."
Visual consciousness arises through these five conditions:

with the eye as its basis, with visible forms as its object of attachment, with light for the sake of observation, and with space for the sake of non-obstruction; thus, mental attention initiates various activities, and by means of these conditions, visual consciousness is produced.
If the conditions—the eye, visible forms, illumination, space, and mental attention—do not come together, visual consciousness does not arise.
Yet, the eye does not form the thought:
"I am able to serve as the basis for visual consciousness."
Form, too, does not form the thought:
"I am able to cause consciousness to become attached.
Nor does clarity form the thought:
"I can cause consciousness to attain contemplative observation," nor does space form the thought:
"I can cause consciousness to be without obstruction."
The mind also does not form the thought:
"I am able to cause consciousness to arise and act.
Consciousness also does not form the thought:
"I am able to arise from various conditions.
However, visual consciousness actually arises from the conjunction of various conditions.
It is the same for all the sense faculties arising in succession; they are all like this.
"Furthermore, there is no dharma that passes from this life to a future life; it is produced solely by the fruits of karma, conditions, and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
It is like a bright mirror reflecting a face: the face appears within the mirror, yet in reality no face enters into the mirror, for it is manifested through false conceptualization and conditions."

Furthermore, it is like the full moon high in the void, forty-two thousand yojanas from the earth, whose reflection appears in all waters; yet the moon does not set there to be born anew in these waters—it appears merely through the power of false conceptualization and causal conditions.
"Furthermore, it is like taking fire: when fuel is obtained, it burns; when the fuel is exhausted, it is extinguished.

Moreover, Śāriputra, there is no sentient being that goes from this world to a future world, nor does one come from a future world to this world; rather, by means of the bonds of karma, the seed of consciousness is formed and takes birth in various places."
Entrusting itself to the womb, it gives rise to the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

This law of dependent origination is from the beginning without a master, without a self, without grasping, and without relinquishing; it is like space, like a magical illusion, and lacks any substantial reality, yet the retribution for good and evil karma does not perish.
"Furthermore, the twelve links of dependent origination are also explained by means of five points. What are these five?
They are: impermanence, non-interruption, non-cessation, a small cause producing a great fruit, and similarity."
What is impermanence?
It means that when these aggregates cease, those aggregates arise; cessation is not arising, and arising is not cessation. Because arising and cessation are distinct, it is called impermanence.
What is meant by "not severed"?
It refers to the way a scale rises and falls: as this ceases, that arises; thus it is said to be "not severed.
What is meant by "not extinguished"?
This means that because the karmic causes performed by sentient beings within the realm of beings never perish, how can there be many fruits from few causes?
It means that whatever cause one creates is like a field; because of single-minded diligence and effort, the fruits obtained are vast and manifold.
What is meant by "resemblance"?
It means that because the karma created as a cause does not yield a different retribution, it is called "resemblance.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:
As the Buddha has said:
"If there is one who can contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, this is called right contemplation and right wisdom.
What is right contemplation and right wisdom?

This means that when contemplating what arises throughout the three periods of past, future, and present, one does not form conceptions of existence or non-existence; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.

If śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or people of the world can contemplate this dharma as non-arising, non-ceasing, unconditioned, uncreated, without grasping, without relinquishing, non-perverted, quiescent, stilled, and devoid of intrinsic nature—if they can thus see the dharma, knowing it with quiescence, free from illness, free from wounds—then my vision will be eliminated in the space of a mere blink; like the head of a tāla tree being cut off, it shall not grow again.
This is the attainment of the dharma that is neither born nor extinguished. Śāriputra!

Such a person has attained the perfection of *dharmakṣānti*; the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān shall bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*.

When the Bodhisattva Maitreya had thus spoken this Dharma, the Venerable Śāriputra, along with the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, rejoiced and accepted it with faith; they prostrated themselves and withdrew.
The Mahāyāna Śālistamba Sūtra (The Rice Seedling Sutra)
